questions.q: What are the two parts of an OKR?
a: A longer-term objective and concrete key results
A yearly budget and a quarterly sales target
A mission statement and a list of competitors
A personal goal and a team reward
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes objectives as the vision you aim for and key results as the concrete steps to get there.

questions.q: How should you handle progress on your key results?
a: Record it frequently and review how it serves the objective
Track it once a year when setting new objectives
Only measure it after the objective is achieved
Delegate all tracking to someone outside the team
questions.why: Lesson 1 recommends frequent progress records plus occasional reviews of how they advance the objective.

questions.q: Which four choices does an OKR review offer?
a: Continue, update, start or stop
Expand, shrink, pause or sell
Plan, do, check or act
Lead, follow, delegate or quit
questions.why: Lesson 2 lists continue, update, start and stop as the ways to modify OKRs after a review.

questions.q: How do committed objectives differ from stretch objectives?
a: Committed ones must be fully met, while stretch ones are ambitious and may fail
Committed ones are optional, while stretch ones are mandatory
Committed ones apply to individuals, while stretch ones apply only to leaders
Committed ones last a year, while stretch ones last a week
questions.why: Lesson 3 says committed objectives need 100% completion, whereas Google’s stretch goals may fall short.

questions.q: What does the moon landing illustrate about goal setting?
a: Stretch goals can motivate people to achieve more than they thought possible
Only governments can attempt genuinely ambitious projects
Goals should stay modest so that failure is avoided
Big goals work only when resources are unlimited
questions.why: Lesson 3 uses NASA’s moonshot to show that aiming high boosts motivation, engagement and productivity.
